extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for finding, collecting, killing, cleaning, labelling, packing, and storing marine, freshwater, and land shells for an amateur collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marine shells — ways of obtaining
rubrics_metrics.description: “Marine Shells may be obtained, 1st, by searching on and under rocks at low water, or on coral reefs, among seaweed attached to them, or floating on the sea, or on a sandy beach. Bivalves may be found by digging in the sand, or mud, on a beach, or at the mouth of a river: their presence is generally indicated by a circular breathing hole in the sand. 2nd. By dredging…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search under rocks and seaweed at low tide and after storms (storms often cast up deep-sea shells); dredging for deep-sea shells. For bivalves, dig where circular breathing holes are visible. Specific handling notes: limpets should be detached with a thin blade passed quickly under the shell (careful not to break edges). Small shells on seaweed will drop off in a vessel of cold fresh water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshwater shells — capture method & habitats
rubrics_metrics.description: “We now come to the freshwater shells, which we capture best by means of a perforated scoop, whether they are on the waterweeds or hidden in the sand or mud of the bottom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect in rivers, lakes, ponds, marshes, reservoirs: univalves chiefly on banks, reeds and plants; bivalves generally at the bottom, among stones or buried in sand or roots of aquatic plants. Use a perforated scoop to capture specimens from weeds or bottom substrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land shells — habitats, seasonality, and microhabitat search
rubrics_metrics.description: “These (land shells) mostly abound in a chalk or limestone district, and in moist and wooded situations. Some species inhabit low and damp spots, roots of trees, hollows and crevices of rocks and walls; some lie under stones or pieces of wood, or in the earth; others climb shrubs… They come out early in the morning, and after rain. Some bury themselves in moist places during the dry season, or burrow under leaves, grass, or stones, often closing the mouths of their shells with a white secretion to prevent evaporation during the period of hibernation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search chalk/limestone districts, shady/moist woods, under stones/logs, tree trunks, crevices, hedgerows, and after rain or early morning when activity is highest; collect buried or hibernating specimens by probing leaf litter and soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer live shells when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: “In all cases ‘live shells’, i.e. shells in which the animal is alive, are to be chosen; but, when these cannot be procured, ‘dead shells,’ which have not lost their lustre, or their colour, especially those of rare species, should be preserved.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select live specimens for best preservation and identification; accept dead specimens only if colour and lustre remain. Prioritize live collection for rare species where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect smallest and juvenile specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: “The smallest shells, especially of land species, and young imperfect shells should be collected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include minute and juvenile specimens in collections (they are important for species understanding and variation). Use careful search and appropriate containers for tiny shells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning rule — minimal cleaning only
rubrics_metrics.description: “No attempt should be made to clean them, or to remove the furry skin, more or less thick, with which they are often covered, beyond removing with a soft brush any mud or sand adhering to them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not aggressively clean or strip periostracum/epidermis; only remove loose mud/sand with a soft brush to avoid damaging natural surface, colour, or lustre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Killing/preserving land and freshwater specimens (boiling method)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The animals of Land and Freshwater shells may be killed by immersing them for a few minutes in boiling water, after which the bodies may be easily extracted whole with any suitable instrument, e.g., a fork or a pin, according to size.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief immersion in boiling water for land/freshwater univalves to kill and ease removal of soft parts; then extract body whole with appropriate tools. Afterward bury or dry as described, or drown in cold water and air-dry if preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hot water with marine shells
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hot water should not be used with marine shells: it often destroys their lustre.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not kill/clean marine shells with hot water. Use alternative preservation methods (e.g., burying to dry, cold-water drowning where appropriate) to protect glossy surfaces and colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying / rotting / burial method for removing soft parts
rubrics_metrics.description: “They should be buried, if time permits, in sand, or other dry material, until the animal dries up (in small shells) or rots (in large specimens); or they may be drowned in cold fresh water, and hung up in the air to dry or rot away.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After killing (or when collecting dead live specimens), bury shells in dry sand to allow bodies to dry/decay naturally, or drown in cold fresh water and hang to dry; for large specimens allow rot then wash out decayed matter. Choose method appropriate to shell type and preservation of surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operculum handling and replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the latter, the decayed matter should be washed out, and the operculum, if any, replaced and fixed, say, on cotton filling the shell. This applies equally to land shells.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When internal organic matter has been removed, rinse and replace the operculum; secure it inside the shell (e.g., on cotton) so it remains in correct position for display and long-term preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid injuring mouth edges and hinge ligaments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Care should be taken not to injure the edge or lip of the mouth of univalves, or the ligament of the hinge of bivalves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle shells gently to preserve diagnostic features: do not chip lips or damage hinge ligaments. If a bivalve gapes or ligament is broken, close and tie valves together; if ligament is dry/stiff, soften by placing in water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record locality and dredging depth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The localities in which each species is found should be noted, and, in the case of dredging, the depth of water.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always record precise locality (and depth for dredged specimens) on a small slip accompanying the specimen to preserve provenance data for scientific and collection value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packing shells for transport
rubrics_metrics.description: “All solid shells may be wrapped in one or two folds of paper of any kind. Fragile and minute shells should be put, generally separately, into a box or bottle—with or without cotton, as required. Such packets may be heaped up in any box, heavy shells at the bottom, without pressure, and any blank filled at the top with paper or other elastic material. Sawdust injures the lustre of many species.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrap solid shells in paper; place fragile/minute shells individually in boxes or bottles with cotton as needed. Pack heavy shells at bottom, avoid pressure, fill voids with soft material, and do not use sawdust which can damage lustre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-cabinet arrangement and labelling
rubrics_metrics.description: “The tinier shells may be kept in small glass tubes with corks (such as used for homœopathic medicines), and the medium sized ones in the trays of common matchboxes, these being arranged in large shallow glass-covered trays… In all cases the name, and the place where the shells were found, should be written on a small slip of card placed in the tube or tray. It is not well in most cases to fasten the shells on card, but if this is done gum tragacanth is best. The collection should be kept free from damp and from dust.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small glass tubes and matchbox trays in shallow glass-covered trays as a cabinet substitute. Label each specimen with name and locality on a small slip. Prefer not to glue shells to card; if gluing, use gum tragacanth. Store collections in dry, dust-free conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine minute Pupæ with a magnifier
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the Pupæ should be examined with a magnifier.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a magnifying glass to inspect minute shells (Pupæ) to see diagnostic features like denticles and striations that are otherwise hard to detect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator signs for bivalves in sand
rubrics_metrics.description: “Bivalves may be found by digging in the sand, or mud, on a beach, or at the mouth of a river: their presence is generally indicated by a circular breathing hole in the sand.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for circular breathing holes in sand/mud as a practical field sign for locating buried bivalves before digging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for detaching limpets
rubrics_metrics.description: “Limpets, etc., should be detached with a thin blade passed quickly under the shell, taking care not to break the edges.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a thin, quick-understroke with a blade to detach limpets from rock; take care to avoid chipping or breaking the shell edge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of continental naming and variety vs species
rubrics_metrics.description: “If they receive shells from the Continent, mere varieties are there often named as separate species and variations considered as definite varieties. This is especially the case with Helicella virgata.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when treating continental material: what may be named a distinct species abroad can be merely a variety. Verify identifications with local references and record provenance to avoid taxonomic confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire good reference books early
rubrics_metrics.description: “Two books on shells should be procured at an early stage of the collector’s career, which will give not only minute descriptions of all our land and freshwater shells and their varieties, but also plates of illustrations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain recommended identification manuals early (e.g., Collector’s Manual by L. E. Adams; Rimmers’ Land and Fresh Water Shells) to aid accurate identification and recognition of varieties and diagnostic features.
